title: Which car has the smallest carbon footprint as the energy system changes?
citation: Šimaitis, J., Lupton, R., Vagg, C., Butnar, I., Sacchi, R. & Allen, S. (2025). Communications Earth & Environment 6, 476.
takeaways: A car's footprint depends on when its energy is made, so the use phase should be time-adjusted.
Electricity decarbonises fastest in every scenario, so BEVs came out 32–47% below hybrids.
FCEVs won only in the 1.5 °C scenario, thanks to carbon-negative BECCS hydrogen.

review.q: Why does a typical LCA overstate a BEV's footprint?
review.a: It uses today's grid for all 10–20 years of driving, though the grid gets cleaner.
The lifetime distance at which a BEV's whole-life footprint drops below a hybrid's.

title: If battery metals get expensive, do fewer people buy electric cars?
citation: Wang, H., Feng, K., Wang, P., Yang, Y., Sun, L., Yang, F., Chen, W.-Q., Zhang, Y. & Li, J. (2023). Nature Communications 14, 1246.
takeaways: In GCAM, metal prices reach EV uptake through battery cost, then cost per passenger-km, then the logit share.
A High price surge cut China's EV share from 49% to 35% (2030) and from 67% to 51% (2060), raising 2020–2060 road CO2 by 28%.
Cobalt-free chemistries (LFP, LMO) and recycling soften the blow; passenger cars are hit hardest.

review.q: Why can a 7–10% rise in EV cost cut the EV share by about 14 points in GCAM?
review.a: The logit with a large exponent turns small cost gaps into big share shifts, especially when options are close in cost.

review.q: Why did LFP batteries soften the impact of the metal price surge?
review.a: LFP contains no cobalt or nickel, so only the lithium price rise reaches the battery cost.

title: Will hydrogen fuel trucks and ships, or mostly factories?
citation: O’Rourke, P., Mignone, B. K., Kyle, P., Chapman, B. R., Fuhrman, J., Wolfram, P. & McJeon, H. (2023). Environmental Science & Technology 57(48), 19508–19518.
takeaways: In below-2 °C runs, hydrogen reached 10–22 EJ in 2050 (2–4% of final energy), and industry used more than transport in most cases.
Cheaper end-use technology (e.g. fuel-cell trucks) raised hydrogen use by 70–84%; adding pipelines and trucks added under 2 EJ and mainly shifted production from on-site to central plants.
Green on-site electrolysis was the largest source (36–69%); a 1.5 °C goal more than doubled hydrogen use to 30–48 EJ.

review.q: In O’Rourke et al. (2023), what mattered more for how much hydrogen gets used: delivery options or end-use costs?
review.a: End-use technology costs. Delivery options mainly changed where hydrogen was made (on site vs central plants).

review.q: Why was most green hydrogen made on site in GCAM’s results?
review.a: On-site electrolysis skips the cost of trucking or piping hydrogen, which is large per unit; over 90% of green hydrogen was on site.

title: When the US switches to electric cars, what happens to the rest of the energy system?
citation: Sadavarte, P., Shindell, D. & Loughlin, D. (2025). PLOS Climate 4(10), e0000714.
takeaways: A system-wide (consequential) run counts knock-on effects: more power plant output, less refining, shifted fuel prices.
With 75% BEV sales by 2050 (vs 31% in REF), car CO2 fell about 54%, fuel production CO2 about 19%, and power CO2 rose only about 6%; US CO2 was 4,010 vs 4,200 Tg.
A BEV starts about 30% higher in CO2 (battery making) but catches up in about two years; car NOx, SO2 and CO fell by about half, with a small coal-driven SO2 bump around 2030.

review.q: In Sadavarte et al. (2025), why did US CO2 fall only about 5% when car CO2 fell by about half?
review.a: Cars are one slice of national emissions, and the power sector emitted about 6% more; other sectors stayed the same.

review.q: How do you work out a BEV's carbon breakeven time?
review.a: Divide the extra CO2 from making the battery by the CO2 the BEV saves each year compared with a petrol car.

title: Can all of transport, even planes and ships, reach zero CO2 by 2050?
citation: Speizer, S., Fuhrman, J., Aldrete Lopez, L., George, M., Kyle, P., Monteith, S. & McJeon, H. (2024). Nature Communications 15, 4439.
takeaways: Under a 1.5 °C cap, the high-ambition case took transport's direct CO2 to zero by 2050; medium and low left 39 and 157 Gt CO2 for 2050–2100, costing roughly $7–14 or $27–54 trillion to remove with DAC.
Electricity led most modes; international shipping was the one mode led by hydrogen, and long-haul flights relied on clean liquids (over 88%), mostly FT biofuel, since e-fuels stayed under 16%.
With one world cap, weak transport ambition shifts cuts to industry and power (128 and 74 Gt CO2 over the century), and shrinks flying and shipping by 40% or more through the carbon price.

review.q: In Speizer et al. (2024), why did long-haul flights run mostly on biofuel even in the high-ambition case?
review.a: Batteries and hydrogen turbines were far too costly for long routes (break-even over $1,300 per t CO2), so drop-in clean liquids won, and FT biofuel was much cheaper than e-fuel.

review.q: How do you work out a break-even carbon price for a clean technology?
review.a: Divide its extra cost per unit of service by the CO2 it saves per unit. Example: $18 extra ÷ 0.06 t saved = $300 per t.

title: When the world prices carbon, why is freight so hard to clean up?
citation: Muratori, M., Smith, S. J., Kyle, P., Link, R., Mignone, B. K. & Kheshgi, H. S. (2017). Environmental Science & Technology 51(6), 3526–3533.
takeaways: Freight has tracked GDP with little sign of decoupling yet; with no policy, GCAM's freight energy grows 4–7× by 2100 and its CO2 grows faster than passenger transport or other end uses.

Under the strictest target (LCP 2.6), cumulative freight CO2 to 2100 fell 68–73% versus no policy, mostly through cleaner liquid fuel (biofuels with CCS), then less freight; mode and technology shifts did little.
Slower freight growth matters: 2100 direct freight CO2 was about 40% lower with no policy, and mitigation costs were 17–49% lower, depending on the target.

review.q: In Muratori et al. (2017), which lever cut freight CO2 most under a strict carbon price?
review.a: Lower carbon intensity of liquid fuel, especially biofuels made with CCS; price-driven drops in freight came second, and mode shift was small.

review.q: Why is freight cut less than buildings under the same carbon price in GCAM?
review.a: Buildings can switch to clean electricity easily; freight relies on liquid fuels and has few cheap low-carbon mode or technology options.

title: Planes need liquid fuel. Can biojet fuel clean up flying?
citation: Wise, M., Muratori, M. & Kyle, P. (2017). Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment 52(A), 244–253.
iam: GCAM v4 (global, with a separate jet fuel sector)
takeaways: With no climate policy, GCAM's demand for flying grows 4× from 2010 to 2050, while jet fuel and aviation CO2 grow about 3× because planes get more efficient.
With fossil jet fuel only, a carbon price that halves 2050 energy CO2 (vs 2005) cuts aviation CO2 by only about 10–20%, and only by slowing the growth of flying.
Biojet, mostly FT from woody biomass, cuts aviation CO2 much more when made with CCS (net about 50% below today by 2050), while using only about 10% of all bioenergy.

review.q: In Wise et al. (2017), why did a carbon price cut aviation CO2 so little when only fossil jet fuel was available?
review.a: Planes had no clean fuel to switch to, so the only response was flying less; CO2 per litre stayed the same.

review.q: Why does biojet made with CCS count as negative emissions?
review.a: Plants took CO2 from the air; the fuel's carbon returns in flight, but the CO2 captured at the plant is stored underground, so overall CO2 leaves the air.
